extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists submitting work to literary agents
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing a novel submission package (manuscript pages, synopsis, and pitch/query letter) to send to literary agents. Focuses on presentation, opening strength, early-chapter editing, synopsis and pitch letter content and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format your work properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an unfussy font (Times New Roman 12 point recommended), 1.5 or double spacing, paragraphs indented (not spaced between), dialogue properly formatted; number your pages and put your name on them; do not include a copyright notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting work cleanly and professionally makes a big difference because agents have a large volume of reading; poorly formatted, densely packed pages or tiny fonts make it harder to read and give a bad impression. Ensure readability (indented paragraphs, correct dialogue formatting) and basic housekeeping (page numbers, name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Put a title on the material
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a working title on your submission rather than leaving the novel title-less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good title can make an agent sit up; a title-less novel lacks identity and makes it harder for agents to refer to or discuss the project. If you don't have a final title, a working title is better than none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish up your first page
rubrics_metrics.description: The first page should introduce a character, establish where and when the story is happening, and show straight away what genre the story is in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents may not read far unless the opening draws them in, so avoid clichéd openings (e.g., a person waking up or staggering about with a hangover) and unnecessary showy language or super-long sentences. You don't need extreme action, but give the reader something intriguing that gets the story going.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tighten up your early chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: Edit the opening chapters so the first chapter sets out the story and asks the key question driving the novel; keep scenes/sequences generally to about 1000–1500 words; avoid front-loading lots of character backstory before the action starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most agents ask for the first three chapters or ~3000 words (check specific requirements). Trim lengthy scenes (e.g., a single 3000-word conversation) and move the plot forward from the off, showing characters as they enter the action. Read the work aloud to check flow, and thoroughly check spelling and grammar because typos suggest lack of care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check agent-specific submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify each agent or agency's own guidelines (e.g., how many chapters/words to send) on their website before submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While many agencies request first 3 chapters/about 3000 words, individual agents may differ—follow their stated format, length, and any other procedural instructions to avoid having your submission discarded or delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a one page synopsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a one-page synopsis with the title at the top, opening with one or two lines that function as a pitch or state the key question your story revolves around, then set out the whole story briefly in a readable way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't get bogged down in excessive detail or name-check lots of characters; include key plot points. Agents differ on whether to include big reveals at the end, so decide what feels right; regardless, the exercise helps you test the novel's structural bones. Some agents don't read synopses, others consider them crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your pitch letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the pitch/query letter short (about three paragraphs, well within one page). Address a specific agent, include a one- or two-line pitch, mention the genre (if known), and briefly introduce the story and protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating the synopsis. Explain concisely why you are sending to that particular agent (show you've researched them). If there are obvious, current comparable titles you may mention them (avoid grandiose comparisons to literary greats). Include just a few relevant personal details (not your whole life story)—e.g., notable writing prizes, relevant courses, or profession that informs the book—but keep it brief.
